3.4. Primary Experience Module
[id=S3.SS4.p1.1] For clusters with a cognitive gap below the threshold τ∗\tau^{*}, the data serve only as a fine-tuning of the model’s cognition, and the risk of noise is controlled. Thus, we directly internalize the new knowledge or skills contained in user logs into the model by training a LoRA based on preference data constructed in the preprocessing stage.
[id=S3.SS4.p2.1] Cluster-specific Preference Learning.
We partition the data into training and validation sets. For clusters exhibiting low to moderate gaps, we train an Expert LoRA Δ​θC\Delta\theta_{C} on the training set using the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023)) loss. To improve training stability, we add a negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss on the chosen responses with the same weighting ratio.
This module enables the model to internalize newly observed capabilities from user logs directly into its parameter space.
[id=S3.SS4.p3.1] Simulation-based Validation.
We construct a simulated performance verifier from the validation set to assess training efficacy. For each query qiq_{i}, using ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} as context, we apply an LLM-as-Judge to compare yiC∼πθ+ΔθC(⋅|qi)y_{i}^{C}\sim\pi_{\theta+\Delta\theta_{C}(\cdot|q_{i})} with yi∼πθ(⋅|qi)y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q_{i}) at the end of each training epoch. We compute the WinRate of each checkpoint relative to the base policy and retain the best expert module only when the highest win rate WinRateb​e​s​t>γ\text{WinRate}_{best}>\gamma. Otherwise, we turn to Reflective Experience Construction. Note that we observe a small fraction of reward-hacking behavior during the verification process. Consequently, we perform filtering prior to evaluation. In particular, we remove responses that are empty after stripping newline characters and special tokens, as well as responses that deviate drastically from the original response (e.g., those with a BLEU-4 score (Papineni et al., 2002) below a very small threshold, such as 0.05).
[id=S3.SS5]
3.5. Reflective Experience Module
[id=S3.SS5.p1.1] For clusters with large cognitive gaps or failing in primary experience construction, we train a Critic LoRA Δ​ωC\Delta\omega_{C}, which is designed to provide “pseudo user feedback” ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}} for the model’s initial responses.
The training input consists of a query qiq_{i} and a model response yiy_{i}, while the output is an extracted rule set ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, optimized using a negative log-likelihood loss. We select the checkpoint from the epoch with the lowest validation loss as the final Critic LoRA.
During inference, Critic LoRA provides feedback on the initial output of the base LLM, allowing the base LLM to refine its response. Our experiments demonstrate that, for clusters with high noise risk, this strategy effectively leverages informative signals in the logs and significantly reduces the risk of noise-induced collapse compared to directly training an Expert LoRA.
Moreover, the inclusion of the Reflective Experience Module ensures that UNO’s optimization framework does not become overly conservative, allowing it to reliably leverage valuable signals from user logs even in clusters that have been filtered out by cognitive gap assessment or failed in primary experience construction.
[id=S3.SS6]
3.6. Inference Workflow
[id=S3.SS6.p1.1] During inference, given a new query qn​e​wq_{new}, the optimized policy πθ′\pi_{\theta^{\prime}} first computes the euclidean distance between qn​e​wq_{new}’s embedding and the query embeddings of all cluster centroids, and assign qn​e​wq_{new} to the cluster C∗C^{*} whose centroid is closest. The response generation procedure then varies according to the characteristics of C∗C^{*}:
[id=S3.I1.i1] •
[id=S3.I1.i1.p1.1] Primary Path: If C∗C^{*} corresponds to a primary experience cluster, the response is sampled directly from the associated Expert LoRA:
y∼πθ+Δ​θC∗(⋅|qn​e​w)y\sim\pi_{\theta+\Delta\theta_{C^{*}}}(\cdot|q_{new}).
[id=S3.I1.i2] •
[id=S3.I1.i2.p1.1] Reflective Path: If C∗C^{*} is a reflective experience cluster, a two-stage generation strategy is employed:
yinit∼πθ(⋅|qn​e​w)y_{\text{init}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q_{new}), ℛ^∼πθ+Δ​ωC∗(⋅|qn​e​w,yinit)\hat{\mathcal{R}}\sim\pi_{\theta+\Delta\omega_{C^{*}}}(\cdot|q_{new},y_{\text{init}}), and
y∼πθ(⋅|qn​e​w,yinit,ℛ^)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q_{new},y_{\text{init}},\hat{\mathcal{R}}).
[id=S3.I1.i3] •
[id=S3.I1.i3.p1.1] Fallback: If qn​e​wq_{new} is an outlier, i.e., having a distance to the nearest centroid exceeding a threshold dd, the response is generated using the original policy:
y∼πθ(⋅|qn​e​w)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|q_{new}).

[id=S4]
4. Experimental Setup
[id=S4.SS1]
4.1. Evaluation
[id=S4.SS1.p1.1] We evaluate all the methods on MemoryBench (Ai et al., 2025), the first benchmark designed to assess the performance of user log-driven continual learning frameworks. MemoryBench spans multiple languages, tasks, domains, and datasets. Its log data are generated by a carefully designed User Simulator that produces interaction logs conditioned on each model’s own responses. The simulator outputs are validated via A/B testing, in which human annotators cannot distinguish simulator-generated logs from real user logs.
[id=S4.SS1.p2.1] The benchmark comprises two parts: user logs collected during early stage (the training set) and subsequent new requests (the test set). All strategies are performed on the training set and evaluated on the test set. Since test queries for each task originate from multiple datasets, MemoryBench first computes dataset-specific evaluation metrics and then applies either min–max normalization or z-score to obtain the final task-level performance. For both metrics, higher values correspond to better performance. We adopt the normalization parameters provided by the official repository.
[id=S4.SS1.p3.1] We conduct experiments on four task-based datasets (Short-input–Long-output, Short-input–Short-output, Long-input–Long-output, and Long-input–Short-output). Each dataset contains user logs (dialogue sessions, including verbal feedback from users and model responses) generated from queries in 3–6 distinct data subsets. We evaluate all strategies using two base models: Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) (no-thinking mode) and phi-4 (14B) (Abdin et al., 2024). We also evaluate a lighter-weight variant, UNO-Single, in which the Reflective Path is removed, and responses for clusters that are filtered out are generated directly by the base LLM. Thus, UNO-Single adopts a more conservative optimization strategy without introducing any additional input or output tokens at inference time. For the significance test, we adopt the paired tt-test (Student, 1908).
[id=S4.SS2]
4.2. Baselines
[id=S4.SS2.p1.1] Prior work does not propose a pipeline specifically tailored for user log-driven optimization. In addition to the direct output of the base model, we compare against three related categories of methods:
[id=S4.I1.i1] •
[id=S4.I1.i1.p1.1] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): RAG augments LLMs by retrieving and incorporating relevant external information (Su et al., 2024b; Su et al., 2024a; Tu et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025a). In our setting, we treat each dialogue session as an entry and use the test question as the search query to retrieve relevant user queries from the dialogues.
